title-group.article-title: Assessing the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) in pediatric differentiated thyroid carcinoma

sec.title: Background
sec.p: The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), encoded by the SLC5A5 gene, is essential for iodide uptake and the effectiveness of radioiodide therapy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC). Data addressing the relationship between NIS transcription and protein expression in pediatric DTC remain limited.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of pediatric and adolescent patients with DTC, evaluating NIS protein expression by immunohistochemistry in tumor and adjacent nontumoral thyroid tissues and tumor SLC5A5 mRNA expression by quantitative real-time PCR. Clinical, pathological, molecular, and treatment-related variables were analyzed.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We analyzed DTC samples from 92 patients diagnosed under the age of 19. NIS was present at significantly lower levels in tumor cells than in adjacent nontumoral cells (odds ratio (OR): 106.8; 95% (CI): 30.7–337.5; P < 0.0001). NIS was only detected in 20/92 of tumor samples, while SLC5A5 was expressed in 36/70 of tumor samples. No associations were found between NIS expression or SLC5A5 expression and clinical or histological features, metastasis, iodide-131 (I-131) activity, or treatment response. A dissociation between gene expression and protein detection was observed. Despite reduced tumoral NIS protein expression, most patients achieved an excellent response to radioiodide therapy.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study highlights significant differences in NIS expression between pediatric thyroid tumors and adjacent nontumoral tissue, with a lower proportion of NIS-positive tumors compared with SLC5A5-high cases. No associations were observed between NIS protein detection or SLC5A5 expression and clinical features, histology, tumor aggressiveness, or treatment response.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Pediatric thyroid cancer is the most prevalent form of endocrine neoplasia, although it remains a rare oncological condition in children (1, 2, 3). Pediatric thyroid cancer differs from adult thyroid cancer in terms of incidence, clinical presentation, pathological features, and molecular characteristics (4, 5). Compared with adults diagnosed with differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC), children and adolescents diagnosed with DTC, including the papillary and follicular types, often exhibit a more aggressive form of the disease, characterized by greater extrathyroidal extension, increased involvement of cervical lymph nodes (nodal metastasis), and distant metastases (6, 7, 8, 9). Interestingly, despite these aggressive traits, mortality rates remain low, typically below 2% (2, 3).

Patients with DTC who present with metastases have a greater risk of recurrence. As a result, the American Thyroid Association (ATA) and the European Thyroid Association (ETA) recommend adjuvant treatment with iodide-131 (I-131) following thyroidectomy for patients in moderate- and high-risk groups. This adjuvant treatment strategy aims to reduce the risk of recurrence and mortality associated with the disease while also facilitating patient follow-up (10, 11).

The sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) is a glycoprotein primarily located in the basolateral membrane of thyroid follicular cells and is encoded by the SLC5A5 gene on chromosome 19p13.11. NIS plays a crucial role in the active uptake of iodide from the bloodstream into thyroid cells through NIS (2 Na+/I), which is essential for the synthesis of thyroid hormones (12).

In residual or metastatic thyroid tumors that retain SLC5A5 expression, NIS is a vital component in the response to adjuvant therapy, as it captures I-131 and facilitates cell destruction through ionizing activity mediated by emission of its beta particle (13, 14). Some studies involving adult DTC have indicated that NIS may not be detectable in certain thyroid tumor cells, which may lead to radioiodide resistance (15, 16, 17, 18).

Research focused on the detection of NIS or SLC5A5 expression specifically in pediatric DTC cells has been limited. This research is critical, as pediatric DTC is typically more aggressive than adult DTC and, thus, adjuvant treatment is needed in more than two-thirds of cases (19, 20, 21, 22).

Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the expression of the SLC5A5 gene and the NIS protein and to evaluate its associations with clinical and histological features, metastasis, adjuvant I-131 treatment response, and the final treatment response (dynamic risk) in pediatric DTC patients.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: This was a retrospective cohort study of pediatric patients diagnosed with DTC from 1976 to 2022 at a cancer reference center in Brazil (National Cancer Institute – Instituto Nacional de Cancer – INCA). After approval by the Ethics Committee of the National Cancer Institute – Instituto Nacional de Cancer – INCA (CEP/CONEP 2.146.715 e CAAE 66569517.8.0000.5257), searches of the institution’s physical and computerized records were carried out for pediatric patients diagnosed with DTC.

The study included patients under 19 years of age monitored at the pediatric oncology endocrinology outpatient clinic, with a confirmed revisited histological diagnosis of DTC, with clinical data capable of interpretation and with a tumor sample stored at the institution. Those with a follow-up of less than 6 months, those who did not wish to participate, or those whose tumor samples were insufficient in quantity or quality for analysis were excluded.

Recurrence risk was classified as proposed by the 2015 ATA Pediatric Guidelines (19). The response to treatment at the end of follow-up (dynamic risk) was evaluated as proposed by the adult ATA Guidelines (10) since there is currently no standardized system for assessing the treatment response of pediatric thyroid tumors.

The tissue samples were obtained from the primary tumor tissues obtained during the first thyroidectomy. The evaluation began with the detection of NIS protein by immunohistochemistry (IHC), and then, the remaining material was subjected to analysis of SLC5A5 gene expression by real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR).

sec.title: NIS protein evaluation
sec.p: Slides were prepared in-house using commercially available pre-treated fillers (ImmunoSlide-EasyPath) containing 3-micron sections that were formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE). DTC samples were immersed in xylol (3 times for 5 min each), followed by quick immersion in 100, 90, 80, and 70% alcohol. Excess alcohol was removed in running water for 3 min. Antigenic retrieval was performed in Trilogy Buffer (Cell Marque) at 98°C via the steam process for 30 min. Peroxidase blocking and protein blocking were performed using the NovoLink Max Polymer Detection Kit (Leica Microsystems, Germany) for 5 min each. The samples were incubated with the polyclonal rabbit antibody SLC5A5 (Novolink) at a 1:2,800 dilution overnight in the refrigerator. The slides were incubated with the primary antibody and the polymer (Novolink) for 30 min. To reveal the reaction, DAB chromogen was used for 3 min. Counterstaining was performed with hematoxylin for 30 s. DAB from the Novolink Kit and Haris Hematoxylin were used. After excess hematoxylin was removed in running water, the slides were immersed in 70, 80, 90, and 100% alcohol and xylene. Balsam was used to mount the slides, and cytoplasmic/membrane staining was observed under an optical microscope.

Nontumor thyroid tissue and tracheal tissue served as positive and negative controls, respectively. The latter were retrieved from our institution’spathology archive, having been collected during surgical procedures unrelated to thyroid disease.
NIS expression was recorded as positive or negative. Samples that demonstrated any quantity or intensity of staining were considered positive for NIS detection.
Immunohistochemical evaluation was independently performed by two experienced pathologists blinded to clinical data. Discordant cases were reviewed jointly to reach consensus.

sec.title: SLC5A5 gene expression evaluation
sec.p: RNA was extracted from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples; specifically, one 10 μm thick section per sample was processed with the Purelink FFPE RNA Kit (Invitrogen) following the instructions provided by the manufacturer. The RNA samples were quantified via a Nanodrop (Thermo, USA). cDNA was synthesized from 1.0 μg of RNA from each sample by SuperScript IV Reverse Transcriptase (Invitrogen, USA). qPCR was performed in a 10.0 μL reaction volume with the Quantinova SYBR Green PCR kit (Qiagen, Germany) on a Rotor-Gene thermal cycler (Qiagen). The samples were analyzed in triplicate. The relative level of SLC5A5 mRNA was analyzed via the ΔCt method, and GAPDH was used as the housekeeping gene. The sequences of the primers used in this project were SLC5A-F 5′ ACC​TCA​TCA​AAC​CTC​GGC​TG-3′, SLC5A5-R 5′-GAT​CCG​TAG​ATG​AGT​GAG​AGC-3′, GAPDH-F 5′-CAA​CAG​CCT​CAA​GAT​CAT​CAG​CAA-3′, and GAPDH-R 5′ AGT​GAT​GGC​ATG​GAC​TGT​GGT​CAT-3′.

For gene expression analyses, the positive controls were a DTC sample previously analyzed, and the OE19 cell line was used as a negative control, as it does not express functional NIS. SLC5A5 mRNA expression was recorded as positive or negative. Samples that exhibited any expression (SLC5A5/GAPDH) were considered positive. RNA integrity was confirmed by electropherogram and virtual gel showing 28S and 18S rRNA peaks (in eukaryotes).

All the data and results collected were plotted in Microsoft Excel v.16.0 (Microsoft, USA). For statistical analysis, we used GraphPad Prism 8.0 (GraphPad Software Inc., USA). Absolute and relative frequencies were used to analyze categorical variables. For continuous variables, we assessed the normality of the data and described them as the mean/median, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, and range values. We assessed statistical significance for continuous variables using Student’s t-test or one-way ANOVA in the case of nonparametric data. When normally distributed, the chi-square (X2) test or Fisher’s exact test was performed for categorical variables. A P value <0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between 1976 and 2022, 165 patients under the age of 19 with a diagnosis of DTC were evaluated in our institution’s pediatric clinic. Of these, 92 patients had available samples deemed suitable for the proposed analyses. Figure 1 outlines the exclusion criteria in more detail.

caption.p: Flow diagram describing pediatric patients with DTC (PDTC) evaluated at the institution with the exclusion criteria for the study.

sec.p: Among the 92 patients, 62 were female, with a median age of 14.8 years (±3.7) at diagnosis. Patients were followed up for an average duration of 8.8 years (±6.0).

In terms of histological features, 89 patients had the papillary DTC and 3 had follicular thyroid cancer, and the mean tumor size was 2.7 cm (±1.7 cm). At the time of diagnosis, 69/92 of these patients presented with cervical nodal metastases, whereas 21/92 presented with distant metastases, all of which were lung metastases. According to the Pediatric ATA Guidelines (19) classification, 50/92 of patients were considered to have a high risk of disease recurrence, and 22/92 were considered to have a low risk. At the end of the follow-up period, only 24/92 of patients presented evidence of structural disease, whereas over, half 45/92, presented no evidence of tumors, indicating an excellent response.

In terms of adjuvant treatment, the average cumulative I-131 activity used was 150 mCi (±177.9 mCi), with a range from 30 to 900 mCi. Twenty-one patients underwent more than one round of radioiodide therapy (RIT) treatment. Table 1 provides clinical, histological, and RIT information for the study population.

caption.p: Clinicopathological features, risk assessment, and treatment outcomes of pediatric patients diagnosed with differentiated thyroid cancer who had stored samples. Data are presented as n or as mean ± SD.

tr.td: Treatment response at the end of follow-up

sec.title: NIS detection and evaluation
sec.p: A total of 92 patients had surgical tissue sufficient for the proposed analyses. NIS protein detection was evaluated in both adjacent nontumoral thyroid tissue and tumoral tissue. NIS presented heterogeneous detection, with variations in both the intensity of staining and the number of positively stained cells (Fig. 2).

caption.p: Immunohistochemical detection of the NIS protein in 20 of 92 tumor samples.

sec.p: In the evaluation of adjacent nontumoral tissue, 89 of 92 samples were positive for NIS protein (NIS+), whereas only 20 of the corresponding tumoral tissue were considered positive for NIS (odds ratio (OR): 106.8; 95% confidence interval (CI): 30.7–337.5; P < 0.0001). Figure 2 shows tumor NIS+ samples. Of the 20 tumor samples that were NIS+, all exhibited NIS detection in the cytoplasmic membrane.
No associations were detected between NIS positivity and clinical features, metastasis, RIT activity, iodide uptake, risk group, or treatment response (Table 2).

caption.p: Association of NIS detection and SLC5A5 expression with clinical features, metastasis detection, risk assessment, and response to therapy and radioiodide treatment.

fn.p: NIS, sodium-iodine symporter; ATA, American Thyroid Association; RIT, radioiodine treatment; mCi, millicurie.

sec.title: SLC5A5 gene expression evaluation
sec.p: Following NIS detection, only 70 tumor samples were sufficient for evaluating SLC5A5 gene expression. The RNA extraction yielded a median concentration of 404.9 ng/μL (range: 23.1–2,349.6 ng/μL). The RNA purity, assessed using the 260/280 nm ratio, was a median of 1.87 (range: 1.28–2.02). SLC5A5 gene expression was detected in 36 out of the 70 samples (51.4%) (Table 2). A significant difference was detected between SLC5A5 gene expression and NIS protein detection, with higher expression levels in samples considered NIS+ according to IHC (P = 0.02) (Fig. 3).

caption.p: Association of SLC5A5 expression with NIS protein detection.

sec.p: A heatmap of the 92 patients’ characteristics, including tumor SLC5A5 expression, NIS detection, and treatment response at the end of follow-up, is shown in Fig. 4.

caption.p: Heatmap of the 92 patients’ characteristics, SLC5A5 expression, NIS detection, and the response to treatment at the end of follow-up.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study provides a comprehensive evaluation of NIS at both the transcriptional (SLC5A5 mRNA) and protein levels in one of the largest single-center pediatric cohorts with DTC. We demonstrate that NIS protein detection is significantly lower in pediatric thyroid tumors than in adjacent nontumoral thyroid tissue (89 vs 20 cases, P < 0.0001). Although SLC5A5 mRNA expression correlated with NIS protein detection (P = 0.02), a marked dissociation was observed between relatively preserved gene expression and reduced protein detection in tumor tissues.

Reduced NIS detection in thyroid cancer, including pediatric DTC, compared with adjacent nontumoral thyroid tissue is a consistent finding across multiple studies (23, 24). In pediatric populations, NIS detection appears to vary with age, with lower levels reported in younger children than in adolescents, potentially influencing tumor biology and response to radioiodide therapy (25). These age-related differences may partially explain the heterogeneous clinical behavior observed in pediatric DTC.

The reduced tumoral detection of NIS protein may reflect impaired post-transcriptional regulation, altered glycosylation, defective intracellular trafficking, or increased protein degradation. Recent experimental data indicate that NIS functionality depends predominantly on correct membrane targeting and posttranslational modifications rather than transcriptional regulation alone. These mechanisms may be particularly relevant in pediatric thyroid tumors, which often display molecular and epigenetic profiles distinct from those of adult DTC.

Epigenetic regulation also plays an important role in NIS expression. Hypermethylation of CpG islands within the SLC5A5 promoter region has been associated with reduced NIS detection in thyroid tumors, including pediatric tumors, and may represent an early event in thyroid tumorigenesis (26). This observation supports the rationale for evaluating SLC5A5 gene expression in parallel with protein detection.

To date, the relationship between SLC5A5 mRNA expression and NIS protein detection in pediatric thyroid cancer has not been extensively explored. Although the literature broadly addresses SLC5A5 expression and its prognostic implications in papillary thyroid carcinoma, most data derive from adult cohorts. Several studies have reported discrepancies between NIS mRNA and protein levels in thyroid tumors. Suh et al. (27) demonstrated that in adult PTC, SLC5A5 mRNA expression negatively correlates with SLC2A1 and positively correlates with SLC2A4 expression. Trouttet-Masson et al. (28) reported that although NIS transcripts are detectable in approximately 50% of hypofunctioning thyroid tumors, the NIS protein is frequently undetectable, suggesting posttranscriptional dysregulation or impaired protein maturation. In addition, Peyrottes et al. (29) suggested that intracellular NIS staining observed in some thyroid tumors may reflect nonspecific antibody binding rather than true functional protein expression, implying that actual NIS levels in these cancers are low. Tavares et al. (30) further demonstrated that reduced SLC5A5 expression correlates with diminished NIS localization at the plasma membrane in DTC and is associated with greater tumor aggressiveness and common oncogenic alterations, including BRAF, RAS, and TERT mutations.

Collectively, these studies indicate that discrepancies between NIS mRNA expression and protein detection in thyroid cancer may arise from transcriptional and posttranscriptional alterations, impaired protein localization, and technical limitations of immunohistochemical assessment.

This perspective is clinically relevant, as novel targeted and redifferentiation therapies aimed at restoring NIS expression and function are currently under investigation. These approaches seek to re-enable radioiodide uptake in tumors previously classified as radioiodide-refractory, potentially allowing retreatment with I-131 (31).

Although pediatric DTCs often present with more advanced disease than adult DTC and require adjuvant radioiodide therapy in more than 75% of cases, the low rate of NIS protein detection observed in our study may suggest that the subset of pediatric patients achieving a complete response to adjuvant I-131 therapy is smaller than traditionally expected. Consistent with previous reports (22, 32, 33, 34), only approximately half of our cohort achieved an excellent response at the end of follow-up, while 24/92 had persistent structural disease after a mean follow-up of 8.8 years. Importantly, no disease-related deaths were observed.

Our findings align with adult DTC data and limited pediatric studies, including the seminal work by Patel et al. (35), which demonstrated an association between NIS expression and clinical outcomes in children and adolescents. However, studies simultaneously assessing paired NIS transcription and protein localization within the same pediatric tumors remain scarce. Our data extend existing knowledge by demonstrating that preserved SLC5A5 transcription does not necessarily translate into detectable or functionally relevant NIS protein expression in pediatric DTC.

Despite low NIS protein detection by immunohistochemistry, many pediatric patients achieved favorable responses to radioiodide therapy. This apparent paradox may be explained by intratumoral heterogeneity, partial preservation of functional NIS in subclonal tumor populations, or sufficient iodide uptake capacity despite low overall protein expression. These observations support the continued clinical effectiveness of radioiodide therapy in pediatric DTC while underscoring the limitations of static immunohistochemical assessment as a surrogate for functional iodide uptake.

This study has inherent limitations, including its retrospective design, single-center setting, limited number of tumor samples available for SLC5A5 analysis, and the differing sensitivities of immunohistochemistry and PCR-based methods. In addition, functional imaging correlation was not systematically available for all cases. Nevertheless, given the rarity of pediatric DTC, our cohort provides robust descriptive and translational data and supports the need for future multicenter studies integrating molecular, epigenetic, and functional imaging approaches.

Although no pediatric studies have specifically addressed the role of NIS evaluation in the context of emerging targeted therapies, a deeper understanding of NIS expression and molecular profiles in pediatric DTC may help identify patients most likely to benefit from redifferentiation strategies. NIS assessment may also prove useful for estimating the likelihood of successful ablation following such therapies.

In conclusion, this study highlights significant differences in NIS expression between pediatric thyroid tumors and adjacent nontumoral tissue, with a lower proportion of NIS-positive tumors compared with SLC5A5-high cases. No associations were observed between NIS protein detection or SLC5A5 expression and clinical features, histology, tumor aggressiveness, or treatment response. These findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating and emphasize the need for prospective, multicenter studies to better define iodide handling in pediatric thyroid cancer and to advance personalized therapeutic strategies.
